Chapter 7.2 | States of Matter

Chapter 7.2

How Can We Explain the Properties of Different States of Matter?

Same particles. Different arrangement. Different behaviour.

Why can you squash the air in a syringe, but not the water?

Learning Objectives

What you will be able to do by the end

  • State the physical properties of a solid, a liquid and a gas.
  • Describe how the particles are arranged and how they move in each state.
  • Use the particulate nature of matter to explain each property.
  • Explain why a gas can be compressed but a solid and a liquid cannot.
📓 Now complete your notes: Section 1: Properties of solids, liquids and gases Write the lesson title at the top of Section 1.
Recall

What did 7.1 teach us?

Brownian motion showed us that matter is made of small, separate particles in constant, random motion.

Learn
  • Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
  • It can be grouped by its state: solid, liquid or gas.
  • The spaces between particles are vacuum.Vacuum means empty. Not air, not anything. This matters today, because a gas can be squashed into those empty spaces.
Key Facts
  • Particles move in every state, including a solid.
  • What changes between states is arrangement and movement, not the particles themselves.
Test

What is found between the particles of a substance?

Core concept

How the three states compare

Three properties tell the states apart: definite volume, definite shape, and whether it can be compressed.

Learn
  • A solid has a definite volume and a definite shape, and cannot be compressed.
  • A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape, and cannot be compressed.Pour a carton of juice into a wide bowl. It spreads out and looks completely different, but it is still the same amount of juice. The shape changed. The volume did not.
  • A gas has no definite volume and no definite shape, and can be compressed.Let a balloon go in a room and the air inside spreads through the whole room. It does not stop at the size the balloon was. A gas always fills its container.
Key Facts
  • Only a gas can be compressed. Solids and liquids cannot.
  • Solids and liquids share one property: both have a definite volume.
Test

A substance has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. What is it?

📓 Now complete your notes: Section 1: Properties of solids, liquids and gases Complete the nine boxes of the properties table. Use the exact words from the Learn tab.
Core concept

A solid's particles are packed in an orderly manner

Very closely packed, in an orderly manner, vibrating about fixed positions.

Learn
  • The particles are very closely packed in an orderly manner. They vibrate about their fixed positions.Picture a full box of oranges, packed in rows. Each orange can wobble a little, but it cannot leave its slot. That wobble is what vibrating about a fixed position means.
  • Thus a solid has a definite volume and a definite shape.
  • There is very little space between the particles for them to move closer together. Thus a solid cannot be compressed.
  • The particles are held together by very strong forces of attraction.
Key Facts
  • Solid particles vibrate. They do not stay perfectly still.
  • Say very strong forces for a solid. "Strong" is the liquid's word.
Test

Why does a solid have a definite shape?

📓 Now complete your notes: Section 1: Properties of solids, liquids and gases Fill the solid row: very closely packed, orderly, vibrate, very strong.
Core concept

A liquid's particles slide past one another

Closely packed but disorderly: the particles slide past one another.

Learn
  • The particles are closely packed in a disorderly manner. They move randomly and slide past one another.Think of a crowded corridor between lessons. Everyone is touching, but people keep sliding past each other. Nobody has a fixed spot, yet the corridor is still full.
  • Thus a liquid has a definite volume but not a definite shape.
  • They are a little further apart than in a solid, but there is still little space. Thus a liquid cannot be compressed.
  • The particles are held together by strong forces of attraction.
Key Facts
  • A liquid cannot be compressed. Taking the shape of the container is not the same as being squashed.
  • Liquid forces are strong: between the solid's "very strong" and the gas's "weak".
Test

Why can a liquid be poured but not squashed?

📓 Now complete your notes: Section 1: Properties of solids, liquids and gases Fill the liquid row: closely packed, disorderly, slide past one another, strong.
Core concept

A gas's particles are far apart

Far apart, disorderly, moving randomly and quickly, with a lot of space in between.

Learn
  • The particles are far apart and arranged in a disorderly manner. They move randomly and quickly.Imagine a handful of people in an empty sports hall, all running in different directions. They hardly ever meet, and they cover the whole hall. That is a gas.
  • Thus a gas does not have a definite volume or a definite shape.
  • There is a lot of space between the particles for them to move closer together. Thus a gas can be compressed.
  • The particles are held together by weak forces of attraction.
Key Facts
  • Compression works because of the space between particles, not because the particles themselves shrink.
  • The particles are far apart, not weightless and not gone.
Test

Air in a sealed syringe is compressed. What happens to the particles?
